subject: 1EBA961BF35048008A08B489196F1A6E
introduction: These passages show ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Bahá’u’lláh and the Báb reading the Bible: quoting the Sermon on the Mount to their correspondents, opening the symbols of Genesis, Isaiah and Revelation, explaining what it means that the Son of man came down from heaven or that the sun stood still, and saying plainly which parts of the Old Testament they take as revelation and which as history written later. A hundred of the guide’s 106 quotations are given here. Most of the hundred quotations set beside them are the verses themselves, in the King James wording, so that the reader has the text and its reading side by side. About one in five is another interpreter, or a verse that pulls the other way, and ends in a question: Paul on the wrath of God, Aquinas and the rabbis on the literal sense, Tolstoy on the other cheek, Irenaeus on why there are four Gospels, Spinoza and Paine on who wrote the books of Moses.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads the descent from heaven, the loaves and the whale as symbols. Aquinas held that argument can rest only on the literal sense, and the rabbis that a verse never leaves its plain meaning. What keeps a symbolic reading honest?
He says Jesus meant the saying about the other cheek to educate, not to forbid protecting the flock. Tolstoy took it without exception. How do you decide when a hard saying is limited by its purpose?
“Where does the great Master Jesus speak of the ‘Wrath of God’?” Paul does, and Edwards preached it. What is gained and what is risked by reading the Gospels apart from the rest of the New Testament?

The stories of the Torah are called history written after Moses, Esther a mere story, and some accounts of David inaccurate. Spinoza and Paine said similar things and drew other conclusions. What makes the difference?

The children of the Kingdom are cast out while others come from east and west. Paul warns the newcomers not to boast. How should people who believe they have recognized something speak about those who have not?
Luke has “Blessed be ye poor” and Matthew “the poor in spirit”; one Gospel says the spirit is willing, a tablet says it rejoices. What do you make of small differences in how a saying is handed down?

outside.why: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá applies this saying to believers who lack love for one another. Here is the saying as Matthew gives it, with what becomes of salt that has lost its savour.
“Many are called, but few chosen.” The words close Jesus’ parable of the wedding feast.
“By their fruits ye shall know them.” Jesus says it of teachers: a good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit.
The talk quotes the saying of the mote and the beam in full. This is the King James wording of it.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá retells the story of the woman taken in adultery. John’s account, with the accusers going out one by one.
“Whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek”: the text ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is explaining, as it stands in the Sermon on the Mount.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá limits the saying about the other cheek: Christ would have stopped the wolf. Tolstoy spent his last thirty years insisting that Jesus meant it without exception. Who decides when a hard saying is to be taken as it stands?
“Freely ye have received, freely give.” The words come from Jesus’ charge to the twelve as he sends them out.
“Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.” Mark’s version, with the reason Jesus gives.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá recalls the shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one. Luke’s telling.

Where does Jesus speak of the wrath of God, and not of “the all-consuming love of the Father for His lost son”? The moment in the parable: when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and ran.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá finds no wrath of God in the teaching of Jesus. Paul, in the same New Testament: the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness. How should a reader weigh the Gospels against the Epistles?

The Father of the parable is all love. Jonathan Edwards preached in 1741 a God who holds the sinner over the pit as one holds a spider over the fire. Both men were reading the same Bible; what was each looking for?
May you be able “to expound with knowledge the words of the Holy Bible”. Philip asked a traveller reading Isaiah: understandest thou what thou readest? How can I, except some man should guide me?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays that she may know “all the hidden symbols of prophetic Scripture”. Augustine could not accept the Old Testament until Ambrose taught him this rule: the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.

The prophets are full of hidden symbols waiting to be opened. The rabbis kept a counter-rule: a verse does not depart from its plain meaning. What stops symbolic reading from finding whatever the reader brings?
What oppression is worse than to seek the knowledge of God and “know not where to go for it”? Amos foretold it: a famine, not of bread, but of hearing the words of the Lord.
That the Son of man came down from heaven “has a mystical rather than a literal meaning”. The verse in question, in which he is in heaven while he speaks on earth.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads the descent from heaven spiritually. Aquinas allowed spiritual senses but held that all are founded on the literal, from which alone an argument can be drawn. How does one argue from a symbolic reading?
In John’s Gospel Jesus “hath foretold the advent of a Comforter who shall come after Him”. The promise as John records it.

Certain divines “have interpreted these utterances after their own fancy”. Peter’s letter warns that no prophecy is of private interpretation. Who, then, has the authority to say what a prophecy means?
John the Baptist was asked, “Art thou Elias?” and answered, “I am not.” John’s Gospel gives the exchange.
John said he was not Elias. Jesus said of him: Elias is come already, and they knew him not. How can both be true, and what does the answer teach about “return”?
“The coming of the Son of man is like the coming of a thief.” Paul repeats it to his converts: the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night.
“Be awake lest the Son of Man come and find ye asleep!” Paul draws the conclusion: let us not sleep, as do others; but let us watch and be sober.
The Comforter “speaks not of Himself” and declares what He hears, which the Holy Spirit, having no ear, could not. This is the verse on which the argument rests.
The Advocate of John 16 is said to signify Muḥammad. Muslims have read it so from the beginning, on the strength of this verse of the Qur’an.
The religion of God is “an adorned bride”. The talk quotes Revelation 21; here is the passage.
And Revelation 12, the woman clothed with the sun, which the talk reads of the same religion.
Bahá’u’lláh quotes Isaiah on the new heavens and the new earth. The passage, with its command to be glad.
“This is that Day of which Joel in his Book saith …” The verse of Joel.
Bahá’u’lláh reads Zechariah’s last verse as tidings of a new heaven. The verse, in which every pot in Jerusalem becomes holy.
The first chapter of Isaiah, quoted at length in the tablet: to what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices?
“Heaven” is read as the heaven of Will and “water” as the water of revelation. The verses of Genesis being interpreted.
A spiritual reading of the creation story is very old in the church. Origen, in the third century: who that has understanding will suppose that the first three days existed without a sun?
Joseph “saw in his dream that eleven stars prostrated to him”. The dream as Genesis tells it.
“I am come to give everlasting life.” Jesus’ own statement of what he came for.
The Bible speaks of baptism with water, with the Spirit, and with fire. John the Baptist’s words about the one who comes after him.
“He that drinketh of this water shall never thirst!” Jesus at the well in Samaria.
The five loaves are five Words that satisfied the multitude. Jesus had said in the wilderness what such a reading assumes: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá turns a miracle of bread into a miracle of teaching. Hume would have agreed that the first is not to be believed, and for a different reason. Does the spiritual reading rescue the story or replace it?
The animal nature must be sacrificed, as the sheep was. Paul: present your bodies a living sacrifice, which is your reasonable service.
The story of Cain and Abel has a material and a spiritual meaning. The story’s best-known line belongs to both.
Abel stands for the divine law and Cain for human nature. Augustine read the brothers the same way and built a history on them: two cities formed by two loves.
The Qur’an knows Jonah as Dhu’n-Nún, the man of the fish, and gives his prayer out of the darkness.
Europeans called the story of Jonah a false tale; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads the whale as the people who swallowed him. Jesus had already used the story as a sign.
“If today a general were to stand and say ‘Sun, stand still!’” The passage in Joshua.
“In God’s sight, forced belief is not acceptable.” The Qur’an: there is no compulsion in religion.
The great ages of the patriarchs are read as the duration of their laws. The verse on Methuselah.
Elijah was believed to have “ascended bodily into heaven”. The account in Kings.
“Creation is good.” The verdict that closes the first chapter of Genesis.
Moses “cast off the sandals of allusion” and was called from the Tree. The scene in Exodus.
The tablet quotes Solomon’s prayer for a kingdom such as shall belong to none after him. It is from the Qur’an.
Abraham was sent to Nimrod. The Qur’an tells what became of the fire Nimrod’s people lit for him.
“When will the Egyptian herald bring to the aged one of Canaan glad tidings of Joseph’s garment?” Genesis: when he saw the wagons, the spirit of Jacob revived.
The Báb quotes the Qur’an’s story of Joseph: the bloodied shirt, and Jacob’s “comely patience”. The verse.
In the time of David and Solomon “the fame of their nobility reached all horizons”. The Queen of Sheba: the half was not told me.
Israel reached its height under Solomon. The book that bears his name looks back on all he built and calls it vanity. What does a scripture gain by keeping both verdicts?
Melchizedek “taught Abraham about God”. Hebrews makes much of this figure without father, without mother, without descent.
“The Lord who … brought you out of Egypt.” The words open the Ten Commandments.
Moses and Aaron did not enter the land. Deuteronomy’s last page: I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither.
The stories in the Torah “are historical accounts written after Moses”, since they record later events. Spinoza gave the same proof in 1670, and was cursed for it.

Only the Tablets and the commandments are counted as revealed to Moses; the rest is history. Paine pressed the distinction further: revelation is revelation to the first person only, and hearsay to every other. How far can one sift a scripture and still call it scripture?

“Many of the statements made about [David] are not accurate.” The Bible’s own account spares him nothing, and has a prophet say to his face: thou art the man. Is a scripture more or less trustworthy for recording its heroes’ sins?
“Jesus was a dyer by trade.” The Gospel’s neighbours ask: is not this the carpenter’s son? Where the traditions differ, what would settle the matter, and does it need settling?

There were fifty gospels, and only four were accepted “by the priesthood”. Irenaeus, about the year 180, thought four exactly right: it is not possible that the Gospels can be either more or fewer in number than they are. What was lost, and what was protected, when a canon was closed?
The abomination of desolation is read as Titus, and the flight to the mountains as history. The verses.
“The Lord is the Excellency of Carmel.” Isaiah: the excellency of Carmel and Sharon; they shall see the glory of the Lord.
After two hours “there was not one glimmer of interest” in the rabbi’s face. Jesus on his own generation: we have piped unto you, and ye have not danced.
“Son of God” was also said of the Children of Israel. The verse in Exodus: Israel is my son, even my firstborn.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá shows that “son of God” was a title Israel already bore. The Nicene Creed says of Christ what it says of no people: begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father. What did the church mean to add to the biblical phrase?
“Why callest thou Me good? None is good save One, that is God.” Mark’s account of the exchange.
The words of Ḥabíb the carpenter are from the Qur’an’s chapter Yá Sín.
“They are not my brethren but you are my brethren and kindred.” The scene in Matthew.
“Even shake the dust from off your feet.” The instruction to the twelve.
The coin and its inscription. Matthew’s account, with the answer that has been argued over ever since.
Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s. Peter, before a court: we ought to obey God rather than men. Where does the coin’s lesson end and Peter’s begin?
Christ rode a young donkey into Jerusalem. The evangelists saw in it this verse of Zechariah.
Satan showed Christ the world from a high mountain. The temptation, and the reply.
“Do not be afraid of those people who have control over your body.” The saying in Matthew.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes: the flesh is weak, but the spirit rejoices. In Gethsemane the words are a warning to sleeping disciples: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. What does the saying become when it is used to comfort the sick?
“Let the dead bury their dead.” Luke’s account of the man who asked first to go and bury his father.
The camel and the needle’s eye. The saying, with the disciples’ astonishment.

It is as sure that a rich man cannot enter as that a camel cannot pass a needle’s eye. Paul does not tell the rich to cease to be rich: charge them to be rich in good works, ready to distribute. Is the saying about wealth, or about what wealth does to its owner?
A rich man cannot enter the Kingdom. Proverbs: the blessing of the Lord, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it. How does one Bible hold both?
A rich man asked to be a disciple and was told to keep the commandments. Matthew adds what Jesus said next.
Luke says “Blessed be ye poor.” Matthew says “Blessed are the poor in spirit.” Which did Jesus mean, and does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s use of the saying depend on the answer?
“Happy is the condition of the children.” Jesus rebuked the disciples who kept them away.
“We must become like children.” Paul: when I became a man, I put away childish things. What in a child is to be kept, and what outgrown?
Children “have no worldly ambitions. Their hearts are pure.” Wordsworth: trailing clouds of glory do we come from God, who is our home.
A generous Prince “hath spread a bountiful feast”. Isaiah’s invitation: come ye, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

“You were neither ministers nor monks and you have attained this grace.” Paul warns the newly grafted in: boast not against the branches. How should those who have entered speak of those who have not?
The children of the Kingdom cast out. Jesus told the chief priests the same in other words: the kingdom shall be given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.
“Many shall come from the east and west.” The first half of the saying.
And the second half, which the readings apply to those born into a faith.
A daughter reads the twenty-third Psalm every night before sleep. The Psalm.
“She doesn’t deserve that God should desert her so.” The Psalter has a prayer for that too, the one Jesus used on the cross. What does it mean that scripture supplies the words of complaint?
“Thy Kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth, as it is in Heaven.” The prayer as Jesus taught it.
Jesus quoted Isaiah on those who have eyes and do not see. Isaiah’s commission.
“Do men think that they will be left alone on saying, ‘We believe,’ and will not be tested?” The verse is from the Qur’an.

So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down about a whole day

deuteronomy-moses-died-there.text: And the Lord said unto him, This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed: I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither. So Moses the servant of the Lord died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the Lord.
